claims.claim: Human evolution is the evolutionary history of the human lineage: the physical and behavioral traits shared by all people originated from apelike ancestors and evolved over a period of approximately six million years; paleoanthropology is the scientific study of human evolution, a subfield of anthropology.

The evidence for human evolution comes in three main kinds: human fossils (from more than 6,000 individuals) showing changes in body and brain; traces of behavior such as millions of stone tools, footprints, hearths, and art; and genetics, which shows how closely humans are related to other primates and traces the migrations of Homo sapiens; advances in dating place the finds in time.

Humans and the African great apes (chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas) share a common ancestor that lived between about 8 and 6 million years ago; bipedalism, the earliest defining human trait, evolved over 4 million years ago; large and complex brains, tool making and use, and language developed later, and complex symbolic expression, art, and elaborate cultural diversity emerged mainly during the past 100,000 years.

Natural selection — the process by which traits that help individuals survive and reproduce spread through a population over generations — was developed independently by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, who jointly presented papers introducing it; Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859; 'survival of the fittest' means well matched to one's environment, not biggest or fastest.

Evolution operates on deep time: geologist Charles Lyell's work established that the Earth is millions of years old, providing the timescale needed for slow-acting evolutionary forces to produce major change.

The hominin lineage is a bush, not a ladder: human evolution did not proceed in a straight line; a diversity of species diverged from common ancestors like branches on a bush; most of the 15-20 early human species scientists recognize left no living descendants, several early human species lived at the same time, and Homo sapiens is the only survivor.

Hominins are defined as all species in the direct lineage to humans, including the genera Homo, Australopithecus, Paranthropus, and Ardipithecus; all hominins share bipedal locomotion as a common anatomical-behavioral complex.

DNA evidence for human evolution: the Human Genome Project (1990-2003) sequenced about 99 percent of the human genome; genetics largely confirms the Out of Africa model, with early humans leaving Africa around 100,000 years ago and interbreeding with Neanderthals; mtDNA (passed maternally, without recombination) points to a common matrilineal ancestor (Mitochondrial Eve) who lived in southern Africa about 100,000-200,000 years ago; genetic variation is greatest among African populations, indicating the longest established lineage there.

Evolution describes how species arise, adapt, and become extinct; it does not rank species — there is no single 'goal' species, because natural selection favors traits sufficient for survival in particular environments and the lineage branches rather than climbs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Verbatim support for the 'bush, not a ladder' framing.
positions: No consulted primary source uses the exact phrase 'bush, not a ladder'.

The Smithsonian FAQ states human evolution 'did not proceed in a straight line' and that species diverged 'like branches on a bush,' with Homo sapiens the only survivor; Britannica states the human 'family tree' may be better described as a 'family bush.'
OpenStax 4.7 presents the same shape via the hominin definition and coexisting genera.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the bush framing attributed to the Smithsonian's explanation (branches on a bush) and Britannica's 'family bush'; 'not a ladder' is the lesson's own one-line summary of that shared framing, not a quotation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Dating figures for the origin of Homo sapiens and the Out of Africa migration.
positions: Smithsonian Human Origins states early humans first migrated out of Africa into Asia probably between 2 million and 1.8 million years ago (early Homo), while OpenStax 5.4 says early humans left Africa around 100,000 years ago (modern Homo sapiens) and cites a consensus Out of Africa model traced back to a population in Africa about 200,000 years ago.
OpenStax 5.4 places the matrilineal common ancestor (Mitochondrial Eve) in southern Africa 100,000-200,000 years ago.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids a single precise date for the origin of Homo sapiens: the compressed-clock example says our species appears in 'the final hour or two' of the six-million-year day (about 200,000 years in a 24-hour span), consistent with the OpenStax figures; migration figures are not stated in the lesson.

positions: Smithsonian's Introduction to Human Evolution says most scientists currently recognize some 15 to 20 different species of early humans and that scientists do not all agree about how they are related.
The Smithsonian FAQ confirms several early human species lived at the same time in the past.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states 'some fifteen to twenty early human species' with the Smithsonian attribution and does not claim an exact count or a settled tree.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-4/lessons.json for this topic is generic boilerplate ('Human Evolution is a foundational concept in Anthropology...') with no factual claims about human evolution; its wording was discarded entirely and no draft claim survived into the lesson.
The draft's Eli-10 toolbox-label analogy and its 'applies to a simple scenario' objectives were not supported by any source and were replaced.
correctionsNeeded: All lesson content was written fresh from verified sources; the boilerplate draft contributed no content.

New OpenStax ids were minted for sections 4.4, 4.7, and 5.4 (chapters 4 and 5 were absent from the phase-2 and phase-4 source registries); canonical URLs follow the established naming pattern and were verified via Wayback captures.
The lesson avoids giving a single origin date for Homo sapiens and avoids quoting 'survival of the fittest' without the clarification that it means environmental match, not superiority.

Supports: the working definition (physical and behavioral traits shared by all people originated from apelike ancestors and evolved over approximately six million years); paleoanthropology as the scientific study of human evolution; the common ancestor of humans and African great apes living between 8 and 6 million years ago; bipedalism as the earliest defining human trait, evolved over 4 million years ago; large and complex brains, tool use, and language developing later; complex symbolic expression, art, and elaborate cultural diversity emerging mainly in the past 100,000 years; humans first evolving in Africa, with fossils of early humans from 6 to 2 million years ago coming entirely from Africa; 15-20 early human species recognized by most scientists, with many leaving no living descendants; early humans migrating out of Africa into Asia between about 2 and 1.8 million years ago; agriculture within the past 12,000 years; early human fossils and archaeological remains as the most important clues. sourceRecords.title: 4.4 Evolution in Action: Past and Present — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (2022 edition; 2026 captures display CC BY-NC-SA with a no-LLM-training notice)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. NEW id (no registry entry exists for OpenStax anthropology chapter 4). openstax.org blocks non-JS clients; the canonical URL was confirmed and content read 2026-08-22 via a Wayback capture (web.archive.org/web/2024id_/...). Supports: natural selection accepted as the guiding force shaping why living things are the way they are; Darwin and Wallace developing the idea independently, Wallace's letter to Darwin from the Malay Archipelago, the joint presentation of papers, and Darwin publishing On the Origin of Species in 1859; the components of natural selection (variation, struggle for existence, inheritance, small changes accumulating over long periods); 'survival of the fittest' clarified as environmental match rather than size or speed; Lyell establishing that the Earth is millions of years old, enabling slow evolutionary change; Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics as the discredited alternative. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 4.7 Our Ancient Past: The Earliest Hominins — Introduction to Anthropology
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (2022 edition; 2026 captures display CC BY-NC-SA with a no-LLM-training notice)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER. NEW id (no registry entry exists for OpenStax anthropology chapter 4). Read 2026-08-22 via a Wayback capture of the canonical URL. Supports: the working definition of hominin (all species considered to be in direct lineage to humans, including the genera Homo, Australopithecus, Paranthropus, and Ardipithecus); the hominid/hominin distinction (hominids = all modern and extinct great apes, including humans, gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans); bipedal locomotion as the anatomical-behavioral complex shared by all hominins; anatomical adaptations for bipedalism (valgus angle of the femur, spinal curves, foot arch, realigned big toe); Mary Leakey's Laetoli footprints of three bipedal individuals crossing wet volcanic ash about 3.5 MYA with a modern striding gait; hypotheses for bipedalism's origins (carrying, energy efficiency, thermoregulation) being untestable. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.
